Your relatively short overall career experience stands out as the strongest factor. At 1-5 years, you fall into the most common range among those expected to stay, yet the model sees this limited tenure as pushing you toward leaving, likely because it signals you are still early in your career and may be exploring options.

The second most influential element is that you have received other job offers while working here. This strongly increases the likelihood of departure, as external opportunities often pull people away even when they are reasonably content.

Your time in this specific organization, also 1-5 years, ranks third and mildly reinforces the prediction of leaving. While this duration matches the majority of employees the model expects to retain, it still contributes a small nudge toward exit rather than long-term commitment.

Taken together, these factors outweigh positive signals such as your satisfaction with rewards, recognition from superiors, and useful training you have received. The organization should discuss your career goals openly with you and explore ways to strengthen your sense of stability and growth here. You, in turn, may want to reflect on whether the external opportunities align better with your ambitions than staying and advancing internally.
